body: {"total":8,"records":[{"title":"Haemolysis in blood drawn through peripheral intravenous catheters versus venepuncture in adult emergency patients","authors":"Saarinen-Obi K, Delacroix-Mwangi R, Brandt-Oyelaran T","year":2015,"venue":"Journal of Preanalytical Laboratory Practice","doi":"10.5555/jplp.2015.0211","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared 620 potassium samples from adult emergency patients, 310 drawn through a newly inserted peripheral intravenous catheter and 310 by venepuncture with a needle, over six months in one emergency department. Haemolysis, defined as a haemolysis index above the analyser's rejection threshold, occurred in 19.6 percent of catheter draws and 4.2 percent of venepuncture samples. Catheters of 20 gauge or smaller haemolysed more often than larger ones. Samples were drawn by emergency nurses using standard vacuum tubes. Allocation to method was by clinical situation, not by chance, and the authors could not account for difficult venous access."},{"title":"Catheter-drawn samples collected with a low-vacuum tube or small syringe: haemolysis compared with venepuncture in a randomised crossover study","authors":"Nakamura-Ellis P, Achterberg-Osei L","year":2020,"venue":"Hospital Laboratory Methods Review","doi":"10.5555/ccmr.2020.0147","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In 260 emergency patients who needed both a peripheral intravenous catheter and blood tests, we drew one sample through the new catheter using a low-vacuum tube or a small syringe and one by venepuncture, in random order. Haemolysis occurred in 3.9 percent of catheter samples and 3.1 percent of venepuncture samples, a difference of 0.8 percentage points (95 percent CI -1.4 to 3.0). Potassium results differed by less than 0.1 mmol per litre on average. All samples were drawn by two trained research nurses, which may not reflect routine emergency practice."},{"title":"Pneumatic tube transport and haemolysis index: the effect of tube speed and distance","authors":"Varadi-Holm S, Castellanos-Ruiz M","year":2018,"venue":"Specimen Transport Notes","doi":"10.5555/lal.2018.0063","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We measured the haemolysis index in 1,480 paired samples sent from the emergency department to the laboratory either by hand or by a pneumatic tube system at two speed settings. Haemolysis above the rejection threshold occurred in 2.0 percent of hand-carried samples and 5.6 percent of samples sent at the high speed setting. Reducing the tube speed brought the rate down to 2.4 percent without a clinically important delay in delivery. Longer routes with more bends were associated with higher haemolysis. The study was done in one hospital with one tube system."},{"title":"Blood sampling through peripheral intravenous catheters and haemolysis: a systematic review and meta-analysis","authors":"Rasmussen-Adeyemi J, Lindqvist-Tanaka H, Oduya-Kowalski B, Ferreira-Mbeki S","year":2022,"venue":"Hospital Laboratory Methods Review","doi":"10.5555/ccmr.2022.0305","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We included 24 studies comparing haemolysis in samples drawn through peripheral intravenous catheters with venepuncture samples. The pooled odds ratio for haemolysis with catheter draws was 3.4 (95 percent CI 2.1 to 5.5), with very high heterogeneity (I-squared 88 percent). The effect was smaller in studies using low-vacuum tubes or syringes and in studies with trained collectors. Only four studies were randomised; most were before-after or cross-sectional comparisons at high risk of bias. Definitions of haemolysis ranged from visual inspection to analyser index thresholds, and the authors rated certainty as very low."},{"title":"Haemolysis in paediatric emergency samples by collection method","authors":"Mwangi-Lorenz A, Petit-Harcourt D","year":null,"venue":"Paediatric laboratory medicine conference abstracts","providerType":"conference abstract","abstract":"We reviewed 410 paediatric emergency samples collected through a newly inserted intravenous catheter, by venepuncture or by capillary puncture. Haemolysis above the analyser threshold occurred in 11 percent of catheter samples, 7 percent of venepuncture samples and 16 percent of capillary samples. Catheter draws avoided a second puncture in most children. The abstract does not state when the samples were collected, how collection method was chosen or whether collectors differed between methods, and no full paper has been identified. Results are presented as percentages without confidence intervals."},{"title":"Who draws the sample matters: haemolysis rates by collector role in the emergency department","authors":"Okonkwo-Stroud E, Lemaire-Achebe N","year":2019,"venue":"Journal of Preanalytical Laboratory Practice","doi":"10.5555/jplp.2019.0092","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Across 9,850 emergency department samples over 12 months, haemolysis above the rejection threshold occurred in 2.1 percent of samples drawn by phlebotomists, 7.8 percent drawn by nurses and 9.6 percent drawn by physicians. Most nurse and physician samples were drawn through catheters, so collector role and method could not be separated. After a 30-minute training session for emergency nurses, their haemolysis rate fell to 4.4 percent over the next six months. The comparison was uncontrolled and the training coincided with a change of tube supplier."},{"title":"Monitoring haemolysis by collection site with laboratory information system data: a retrospective analysis of 1.2 million samples","authors":"Grieve-Nwosu R, Haddad-Lindgren T, Kaur-Whitfield A","year":2023,"venue":"Laboratory Quality Indicators","doi":"10.5555/lqi.2023.0018","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We analysed 1.2 million samples from four hospitals using laboratory information system fields for collection site, collector role and transport route. Haemolysis above the rejection threshold occurred in 6.9 percent of emergency department samples and 1.8 percent of inpatient samples. Variation between collection sites was larger than variation between analysers. The data could not identify whether samples were drawn through a catheter, so the effect of collection method could not be estimated. The authors recommend site-level haemolysis rates as a routine quality indicator rather than as evidence about collection method."},{"title":"Recommendations on preanalytical sample quality and haemolysis management from a laboratory medicine working group","authors":"Preanalytical Quality Working Group","year":2021,"venue":"Laboratory medicine consensus papers","doi":"10.5555/lmcp.2021.0004","providerType":"report","abstract":"A working group of 12 laboratory specialists and emergency clinicians reviewed evidence on haemolysis and agreed recommendations by consensus. The group recommends monitoring haemolysis rates by collection location, using analyser haemolysis indices rather than visual inspection, and training all collectors. It makes no recommendation for or against drawing samples through peripheral intravenous catheters because the evidence was judged conflicting. The group notes that reducing repeat venepuncture matters to patients with difficult venous access and to children, and asks laboratories to publish haemolysis rates by site so that practices can be compared."}]}
